R Data Structures and Operations Quiz

Part 1: Vectors

Question 1: Atomic Coercion

If you run my_vec <- c(1, "A", TRUE), what will be the data type of the resulting vector?

Vectors must be "atomic" (all elements of the same type). R forces (coerces) them to the most flexible type. The hierarchy is Logical \(\rightarrow\) Integer \(\rightarrow\) Numeric \(\rightarrow\) Character.

Question 2: Vector Recycling

What happens when you add two vectors of different lengths, such as c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)?

R uses "recycling" to repeat the shorter vector until it matches the length of the longer one. If the longer length isn't a multiple of the shorter one, it completes the operation but gives a warning.

Question 3: Naming Vector Elements

Which function allows you to assign or retrieve labels for individual elements inside a vector?

The names() function is used for vectors and lists. (e.g., names(my_vec) <- c("a", "b")). colnames() is used for matrices and data frames.

Part 2: Matrices & Arrays

Question 4: Matrix Creation

By default, how does the matrix() function fill its data into rows and columns?

By default, R fills matrices down the columns. To fill across the rows instead, you must explicitly set byrow = TRUE.

Question 5: Matrix Properties

Which of the following is true about a matrix in R?

A matrix is essentially an atomic vector with a "dimensions" attribute (dim) attached to it. Because it is atomic, all data inside it must be of the exact same type.

Question 6: Array Dimensions

What does the code my_array <- array(1:24, dim = c(3, 4, 2)) create?

The dim argument for an array is ordered as c(rows, columns, layers/tables). So c(3, 4, 2) means 3 rows, 4 columns, split across 2 separate "layers" or "slices".

Question 7: Matrix Transposition

Which function is used to transpose a matrix (swap its rows and columns)?

The t() function returns the transpose of a matrix or a data frame.

Part 3: Factors

Question 8: Purpose of Factors

What is the primary purpose of the factor data structure in R?

Factors are used for categorical variables (like "Small", "Medium", "Large", or "Male", "Female"). R stores them as integers under the hood, mapped to character labels called "levels".

Question 9: Ordered Factors

How do you tell R that a factor has a specific, meaningful order (e.g., Low < Medium < High)?

Setting ordered = TRUE makes it an ordinal categorical variable, which is highly important for statistical modeling and plotting.

Question 10: Converting Factors to Numeric

If f <- factor(c("10", "20", "30")), what is the safest way to convert it back to actual numeric values?

If you just use as.numeric(f), R returns the underlying integer codes (1, 2, 3) instead of the text values (10, 20, 30). You must convert it to a character first.

Part 4: Lists & Data Frames

Question 11: The Nature of Lists

Which statement is TRUE regarding lists in R?

Lists are the most flexible data structure in R. They are 1-dimensional and heterogeneous, meaning a single list can hold a vector, a matrix, a function, and another list all at once.

Question 12: Single vs Double Brackets

If my_list contains a vector named scores at the first position, what is the difference between my_list[1] and my_list[[1]]?

Think of a list as a train with cargo cars. Single brackets [] give you a train car (still a list). Double brackets [[]] open the door and give you the cargo inside.

Question 13: Data Frame Constraints

Which of the following is a strict requirement for creating a valid Data Frame?

A data frame is technically a list of vectors. For it to form a neat rectangle (table), every vector (column) must be exactly the same length.

Question 14: Adding a Column

Which syntax is commonly used to add a brand new column named Total to an existing data frame df?

The $ operator is the easiest way to extract or create columns. Assigning values to a $ name that doesn't exist yet will automatically create it.

Question 15: Examining Structure

Which function gives you a compact summary of a data frame's internal structure, showing column names, types, and the first few observations?

str() stands for "structure". It is one of the most useful diagnostic functions in R for checking the types of data stored in your data frame.

Part 5: Indexing & Conditional Selection

Question 16: Negative Indexing

What does my_vector[-3] do?

In R, placing a minus sign before an index tells R to drop or exclude that specific index and return everything else.

Question 17: Matrix Indexing

How do you extract the entire 2nd column of a matrix named mat?

Matrix indexing uses [rows, columns]. Leaving the row slot blank (before the comma) tells R to return "all rows" for column 2.

Question 18: Out of Bounds

If x <- c(10, 20, 30), what does R return if you ask for x[5]?

Unlike Python which crashes with an index error, R silently returns NA (Not Available) when you try to access an index that doesn't exist.

Question 19: Logical Vectors

If v <- c(1, 5, 10), what is the result of the expression v > 4?

A logical condition applied to a vector is evaluated element-by-element, returning a boolean vector of the same length. You can use this logical vector to subset the data (e.g., v[v > 4]).

Question 20: The which() Function

What does the which() function return when applied to a logical condition?

which(v > 4) would return c(2, 3) because the 2nd and 3rd elements satisfy the condition.

Question 21: AND vs OR

Which operator is used to evaluate if either condition A OR condition B is true element-wise in a vector?

The single vertical bar | is the vectorized OR operator. (The single & is the vectorized AND operator). The double || and && only evaluate the very first element, usually used in if() statements.

Question 22: Using subset()

What is the main advantage of using the subset(df, condition) function over standard bracket df[condition, ] subsetting?

Instead of typing df[df$Age > 20 & !is.na(df$Age), ], you can just type subset(df, Age > 20). It is cleaner and handles missing values nicely.

Question 23: The %in% Operator

What is the %in% operator used for?

x %in% y returns a logical vector the same length as x, marking TRUE if that element is found anywhere inside y.

Part 6: Missing Values (NA)

Question 24: Testing for NA

Why does x == NA fail to properly identify missing values?

You can never use equality operators with NA. You must use the dedicated function is.na(x) to test for missing values.

Question 25: Calculating with NAs

If x <- c(10, 20, NA, 40), what does mean(x) return?

Most mathematical functions in R will return NA if even one NA is present in the data. You must add the argument na.rm = TRUE to strip them out before calculation.

Question 26: Complete Cases

Which function evaluates a data frame and returns a logical vector marking TRUE only for rows that have absolutely zero missing values?

complete.cases(df) returns a boolean vector you can use to subset the data frame (e.g., df[complete.cases(df), ]). Alternatively, na.omit(df) does the subsetting automatically.

Part 7: Grouped Data

Question 27: The tapply() Function

What is tapply() used for?

tapply(X, INDEX, FUN) takes a vector X, splits it into groups based on the factor INDEX, and applies FUN (like mean) to each group.

Question 28: Splitting Data

Which function breaks a data frame into a list of smaller data frames based on a grouping variable?

split(df, df$category) returns a list where each element is a subset of the original data frame for a specific category level.

Question 29: The aggregate() Function

How does the aggregate() function handle groupings compared to tapply()?

aggregate(value ~ category, data = df, FUN = mean) is highly preferred in base R because its formula syntax is easy to read, and it outputs a clean data frame.

Question 30: By Function

The by() function is an object-oriented wrapper for tapply(). What is it most commonly used to do?

While tapply() works on individual vectors, by(data, INDICES, FUN) splits an entire data frame into subsets and allows you to apply a function (like a linear model lm()) to each subset.
